title: The Gutenberg Bible and a Broken Partnership
summary: Gutenberg's team printed a giant, gorgeous Bible in two huge volumes, so neat that a future pope said you could read it without glasses. But Gutenberg's money partner took him to court, and much of his workshop ended up in other hands. The man who changed the world of books ended his life with a modest allowance of grain, wine and clothes, never rich.

sections.heading: Why Start with a Giant Bible?
paragraphs: By the early 1450s, Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz had a working system: punches, matrices, hand moulds, type metal, oily ink and presses. The team had already printed small things, such as Latin grammar booklets and, a little later, indulgence certificates. Now Gutenberg chose a project so big and so difficult that it seems almost crazy: a complete Latin Bible, in large format, as beautiful as the finest handwritten books in Europe.

Why the Bible? In the Europe of the 1400s, the Bible was the most important book of all. Churches, monasteries, cathedral schools and universities all needed copies for services, study and teaching. The text everyone used was the Latin translation known as the Vulgate, made mostly by Saint Jerome around the year 400. A large church Bible was expensive and took a professional scribe a very long time to copy, often a year or more. If Gutenberg could produce many copies at once, he would have customers ready and waiting, and he could prove to the world that his new art could match the best scribes.

There was also a business reason. Small items like grammar booklets earned some money, but Gutenberg had borrowed huge sums, especially from the Mainz businessman Johann Fust. A big, prestigious book that could be sold for a high price to wealthy churches and monasteries might finally pay back those debts. It was a giant bet.

Today we call the result the Gutenberg Bible. Experts also call it the 42-line Bible, or B42 for short, because most of its pages have 42 lines of text in each of their two columns. Sometimes you will also see it called the Mazarin Bible, because the first copy that scholars studied closely, in the 1700s, belonged to the library of Cardinal Mazarin in Paris.

sections.heading: Building the Biggest Book
paragraphs: Imagine walking into Gutenberg's workshop in Mainz around 1453. The air smells of hot metal, linseed oil and damp paper. In one corner a caster pours type metal into a hand mould. At slanted wooden cases, compositors pick out tiny backwards letters one by one. Big wooden presses creak as pressmen heave on their bars, and stacks of freshly printed sheets hang drying. Historians think the workshop may have had perhaps twenty or so workers and, at its busiest, several presses running at once, though nobody wrote down the exact numbers.

The finished Bible was enormous. It was printed in two large volumes, with roughly 640 leaves, which means about 1,280 printed pages. Each page is about 40 centimetres tall, a little bigger than a large atlas. The text is set in two columns, in a dark, dense style of letters called textura, designed to look just like the handwriting of the best scribes.

Here is a curious detail. The very first pages of the Bible do not have 42 lines per column. The first several pages have 40 lines, then one page has 41, and only after that do the pages settle at 42. Historians think the printers decided to squeeze in more lines after they had started, probably to save paper and vellum, which were very expensive. Two extra lines per column might not sound like much, but across more than a thousand pages, it saved a lot of sheets.

The printers did not set the whole book from start to finish in order. To work faster, they probably split the text into sections and set and printed several parts at the same time on different presses. Setting each page was slow work: compositors had to choose from around 290 different characters, including ligatures and abbreviations, to make every line fit perfectly. Printing all the copies probably took around two years, and the Bible appears to have been finished by about 1454 or 1455.

How many copies were made? Nobody knows for sure. Most estimates fall at about 160 to 180 copies. Of these, roughly three-quarters were printed on paper and the rest on vellum, which is fine calfskin. Some experts estimate about 135 on paper and about 35 on vellum. The paper was high-quality paper imported from Italy, and if you hold a page up to the light you can still see its watermarks, little designs left by the papermakers' moulds, which help experts trace where the paper came from. A single vellum copy needed the skins of a great many calves, by some estimates well over a hundred, so these copies were extremely costly.

sections.heading: Hand-Painted Colour, and Pen Against Press
paragraphs: If you could open two Gutenberg Bibles side by side, you might be surprised: they do not look the same. The black text is identical, because it was printed from the same type. But almost everything else, the colours, the decorations and the big first letters, was added by hand after printing, and that work was done differently for each copy.

In handwritten books of the time, chapter headings and important words were often written in red ink. This was called rubrication, from the Latin word for red, and the person who did it was a rubricator. Gutenberg's team at first tried to print red headings on the press, which meant inking some type red and some black and printing very carefully. It was slow and fiddly, and after a few pages they gave up. In most of the Bible, gaps were simply left in the printed text, and a rubricator filled them in by hand with red and blue ink.

Big decorated initial letters at the beginning of each book of the Bible were also left blank by the printers, so that artists called illuminators could paint them in. Wealthy buyers could pay for gold leaf, curling vines, flowers, animals and even tiny scenes in the margins. Other owners chose plain red and blue letters. Some copies were decorated in Mainz, others in different cities far away, in the local style. That is why each surviving copy is a unique blend of printing and handwork, almost a bridge between the old world of manuscripts and the new world of print.

Buyers also took their copies to bookbinders of their choice, who bound them in wooden boards covered with leather, often with metal corners and clasps. Some copies were bound in two volumes, others in three or four. So when a Gutenberg Bible left the workshop, it was really a stack of printed sheets, and its new owner finished turning it into a book.

To understand what a leap the Gutenberg Bible was, it helps to compare it with a book made the old way at almost exactly the same time and place. In the Great Hall of the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., two glass cases face each other. One holds the library's printed Gutenberg Bible. The other holds the Giant Bible of Mainz, a huge handwritten Bible made in the Mainz area in the early 1450s, while Gutenberg's presses were busy nearby.

The Giant Bible of Mainz was written by a single scribe over a period of more than a year, from April 1452 to July 1453, letter by letter, with a quill pen. It is a magnificent work of art. But when the scribe finished, the world had exactly one new Bible. In roughly the same span of time, or a little longer, Gutenberg's workshop produced somewhere around 160 to 180 copies. Standing between those two cases, you can see the old world and the new world of books looking at each other across the room.

The two books also show how closely early printers copied the look of manuscripts. The printed Bible uses the same kind of dark textura letters, the same two-column layout, the same wide margins and the same habit of leaving room for coloured initials. Gutenberg was not trying to make something that looked new. He was trying to make something that looked exactly like the best handwritten books, only many of them at once. Readers of the time would have found the printed pages familiar, which probably helped them trust the new invention.

Speed did not mean the work was easy or cheap. Every copy still needed paper or vellum, a rubricator, perhaps an illuminator, and a binder. A finished Gutenberg Bible was still a costly object that only a church, a monastery, a university or a rich person could afford. But the most time-consuming part, writing out more than a thousand pages of text, had been done by a machine, and done far more quickly and consistently than any scribe could manage. Every copy had the same words in the same places, which meant that two readers in different cities could point to the same page and line. That kind of sameness would later become one of print's greatest gifts to scholarship.

One more difference is worth noticing. A scribe could make mistakes that appeared in only one copy. A printer's mistake appeared in every copy printed from that page of type. So printers had to check their work carefully before printing, and proofreading became an important job in print shops, as you will see in the next part.

sections.heading: A Future Pope Sees the Pages
paragraphs: One of the most exciting clues about the Gutenberg Bible comes from a letter. Its writer was Enea Silvio Piccolomini, an Italian churchman, poet and diplomat who later became Pope Pius II. In the autumn of 1454 he was in Frankfurt, a big trading city about 40 kilometres from Mainz, attending an important meeting of the rulers of the Holy Roman Empire. Frankfurt also had a famous market fair, where merchants came from far and wide.

On 12 March 1455, Piccolomini wrote to his friend Cardinal Juan de Carvajal in Rome. He described an amazing man he had heard about in Frankfurt who was offering Bibles for sale. Piccolomini said he had not seen a complete Bible, but he had seen some quires, which are bundles of sheets from different parts of the book. He praised the letters as extremely neat and correct, and said that Carvajal would be able to read them easily, even without his glasses.

Piccolomini also passed on numbers. Some people told him that 158 copies had been completed; others said 180. He was not sure which was right, but he had no doubt the copies existed. He added that, sadly, he probably could not buy one for his friend, because buyers had already been found for all of them before they were even finished.

This letter matters for several reasons. It is the earliest known written description of the Gutenberg Bible. It helps date the project, showing that printed sheets were already being shown around by autumn 1454. It tells us that the copies sold quickly, to eager buyers. And it gives us those numbers, 158 or 180, which match the experts' modern estimates. The one thing the letter does not tell us is the name of the amazing man in Frankfurt. It may have been Gutenberg himself, or someone working with him, but we cannot be sure.

sections.heading: The Lawsuit of 1455
paragraphs: Just when Gutenberg's great Bible was finally finished and selling, his partnership fell apart. To understand why, we need to remember the money. Around 1450, Johann Fust had lent Gutenberg 800 guilders, with Gutenberg's tools and equipment as security for the loan. Around 1452, Fust put in another 800 guilders, this time as an investment in what the partners called the work of the books. In total that was about 1,600 guilders, an enormous sum at the time, enough to buy several fine houses in a city.

In 1455, Fust took Gutenberg to court. He demanded his money back, plus interest, and the total he claimed was more than 2,000 guilders. Gutenberg disagreed. He argued, among other things, that the second 800 guilders had been Fust's share in a joint business, not a simple loan he had to repay, and that he had never received all of the money in the way it was described.

We know about the case from a remarkable surviving document called the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument, named after Ulrich Helmasperger, the notary who wrote it down. It records a meeting on 6 November 1455 in a large hall of a monastery in Mainz, where Fust swore an oath about how much money he had handed over. Among the witnesses on Fust's side was Peter Schoeffer, a young man who had trained as a scribe, studied in Paris, and then worked in Gutenberg's own workshop. Gutenberg himself did not attend the final hearing and sent representatives instead.

The court's decision went largely in Fust's favour, ordering Gutenberg to repay a large part of what was claimed. Gutenberg probably could not pay. Historians think that, as a result, much of his printing equipment and probably the type and remaining stock of the Bible passed to Fust. In other words, at the very moment his masterpiece was complete, Gutenberg lost control of much of the business he had spent so many years building.

It is easy to see Fust as a villain, but the true story is more complicated. Fust had risked a fortune on an untested invention and had waited years for any return. Gutenberg seems to have spent money freely on experiments and perfection. Both men were taking big risks, and when the money ran short, the partnership broke. What is clear is that Gutenberg did not get rich from his invention.

sections.heading: Fust and Schoeffer's Masterpiece: The Mainz Psalter
paragraphs: After the lawsuit, Fust teamed up with Peter Schoeffer, who knew Gutenberg's methods from the inside and was a gifted designer of letters. Schoeffer later married Fust's daughter Christina, so the partnership became a family business too. Together they started one of the most successful printing firms of the 1400s.

Their first great book was a Psalter, a book of psalms and other texts sung in church services. It was completed on 14 August 1457. This Mainz Psalter was a showpiece, and it broke several records at once.

First, it is the first printed book to include a printed date. Second, it names its printers: at the end of the book there is a short paragraph, called a colophon, that proudly names Johann Fust and Peter Schoeffer. The colophon also explains, in Latin, that the book was made by a clever invention of printing and forming letters, without any writing with a pen. In other words, the printers were telling the world: no scribe made this, a machine did. Gutenberg's own name never appeared in his books, which is one reason why later generations sometimes forgot his role.

Third, the Psalter is famous for its splendid printed initials in two colours, red and blue, with delicate patterns curling around the large letters. Instead of leaving gaps for a hand painter, the printers printed these decorations on the press. Experts think the initial letter and its decoration were made as separate metal pieces that fitted together like a jigsaw puzzle. Each piece was inked in its own colour, then the pieces were put back together and printed in one go along with the black text. This was one of the very first examples of colour printing in Europe.

The Psalter was printed on vellum, and only about ten copies survive today, which makes it even rarer than the Gutenberg Bible. Fust and Schoeffer went on to print many more books. Fust died in 1466, probably of plague, while on a business trip to Paris. Schoeffer kept the firm going for decades and became one of the leading printers and booksellers in Germany.

sections.heading: Gutenberg's Quiet Last Years
paragraphs: What happened to Gutenberg after 1455? The records are patchy, but it seems he did not give up. He probably kept a smaller workshop of his own, using some of his earlier type and equipment. Several books and smaller printed items from the late 1450s and 1460s have been linked to him or his circle, such as a big Latin dictionary and grammar called the Catholicon, dated 1460, though historians still argue about who actually printed it. None of these works carries Gutenberg's name.

In 1462, Mainz was caught up in a violent struggle between two rival archbishops. In October of that year, the forces of Adolf II of Nassau captured the city. Many citizens lost property or were forced to leave, and printers scattered to other towns, a story you will follow in Part 12. Records suggest Gutenberg was among those who lost out.

Then, in January 1465, came a surprising honour. The same Adolf II, now archbishop and elector of Mainz, named Gutenberg a member of his court. This came with a kind of pension: every year Gutenberg would receive a set of court clothing, about 2,200 litres of grain and about 2,000 litres of wine, and he would be excused from certain city taxes and duties. That is far more grain and wine than one person could use, so some historians suggest Gutenberg may have used it to feed and pay the workers in his shop. Nobody knows exactly why the archbishop rewarded him; it may have been to recognise his invention, or to make peace after the troubles of 1462.

Gutenberg died in Mainz in early 1468. The date often given is 3 February, but the Gutenberg Society notes that this may not be reliable; what we know for certain is that a document dated 26 February 1468 shows he had already died, because his printing equipment was being handed over to a Mainz official, Dr. Konrad Humery. He was probably buried in the Franciscan church in Mainz, a building that was later demolished, so his grave has been lost.

Gutenberg was not famous or wealthy at the end of his life. He had no known children, his name was not printed in his books, and for some time others received much of the credit. Yet by the time he died, printing shops were already opening in Italy and elsewhere, and the art he had developed was spreading across Europe.

sections.heading: Who Was First? A Dutch Legend and a Priceless Book
paragraphs: Because Gutenberg never signed his books, arguments about who invented European printing started early. The most famous rival claim comes from the Netherlands. According to a legend, a man named Laurens Janszoon Coster of Haarlem was the true inventor. The story was written down by the Dutch scholar Hadrianus Junius in his book Batavia, published in 1588, more than a century after the events it describes.

In Junius's tale, Coster was walking in the woods near Haarlem in the 1420s or 1430s and carved letters from tree bark to amuse his grandchildren. He noticed that the letters left marks, and this gave him the idea for printing. The legend even claims that a dishonest workman stole Coster's type one Christmas night and ran off to Mainz with the secret. It is a lively story, and Haarlem built a statue of Coster in its market square. But there is no solid evidence for it. A real Laurens Janszoon did live in Haarlem in the early 1400s and held town offices, but no books printed by him are known. Historians treat the Coster story as a legend, not as history.

Meanwhile, the Gutenberg Bible itself became one of the most treasured objects in the world. About 49 copies survive, some complete and some only partly complete, along with scattered single leaves. They are kept in great libraries in Germany, the United States, Britain, France, Japan and other countries. In 1930 the United States Congress approved the purchase of a large collection of early printed books from the collector Otto Vollbehr, which included a Gutenberg Bible on vellum. That copy, one of only three perfect vellum copies known, is on display in the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C.

Prices for these Bibles became legendary. In 1978 one copy was sold for about 2.2 million US dollars, and the same year the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas acquired its own complete paper copy for about 2.4 million dollars. In 1987 a single volume sold for about 5.4 million dollars, including the auction house's fee. Today, many copies have been photographed page by page and put online, so anyone with a screen can turn the pages of a book once read only by monks and scholars.

Gutenberg's Bible proved that metal type could make books as beautiful as any manuscript, and in large numbers. Fust and Schoeffer's Psalter proved that a printing business could keep going and even improve without its inventor. Gutenberg's workshop was the start, but how did a busy print shop actually turn type into pages, day after day?

deepDive: The Gutenberg Bible raises several puzzles that historians still argue about. The first is chronology. Piccolomini's letter of 12 March 1455 shows that printed quires were circulating in Frankfurt by the autumn of 1454, so the printing must have begun by about 1452. The change from 40 to 41 to 42 lines on the earliest pages, and the early attempt at printing red headings that was soon abandoned, are read as signs of a project being adjusted on the fly to save materials and time. A second puzzle is the size of the edition. Piccolomini heard both 158 and 180; modern estimates usually say about 160 to 180, of which roughly 135 were on paper and 35 on vellum. Survival counts vary depending on what is counted: about 49 copies survive as complete or substantial copies, with further fragments and single leaves, some of which were cut up in later centuries and used to reinforce bindings. A third question is how the workshop was organised. In the 1980s, proton-beam analysis of the ink at UC Davis showed changes between batches that some researchers read as evidence that work began on two presses and expanded to six, and that the final pages used a different ink, possibly after the split with Fust. These are interesting hypotheses rather than proven facts. The Fust lawsuit is also debated. The only detailed record, the Helmasperger Notarial Instrument of 6 November 1455, presents mainly Fust's side, and it does not say outright that Gutenberg lost all his equipment; that is inferred from what Fust and Schoeffer printed next and from the type Gutenberg seems to have kept. Finally, there is the question of credit. Erasmus and others later praised Fust and Schoeffer as the inventors, and Dutch writers promoted Coster. The documentary evidence, especially the 1439 Strasbourg lawsuit and the Mainz records, strongly supports Gutenberg's central role in developing printing with movable metal type in Europe, while Asian printers had developed movable type, including metal type, long before.
funFact: The first pages of the Gutenberg Bible have only 40 lines in each column; the printers changed to 42 lines a few pages in, most likely to save expensive paper and vellum.

check.q: What was special about the Mainz Psalter printed by Fust and Schoeffer in 1457?
check.a: It was the first printed book with a printed date and the printers' names, and it had printed colored initials
wrong: It was the first book ever printed anywhere in the world

It was the first book printed in English
